subject: Science
title: Ravi's Wildlife Adventure: The Amazing Variety of Life
hook: A village boy discovers that living things come in endless shapes, sizes, and ways of life—from tiny insects to giant trees.

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: curious naturalist exploring the village and forest

characters.name: Maya
characters.role: Ravi's sister who loves collecting leaves and insects

characters.name: Forest Guard Dada
characters.role: local expert who teaches about wildlife

slides.title: Diversity in the Living World
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Maya explore their village and nearby forest, spotting insects, birds, plants, fish, and creatures they've never seen before. Forest Guard Dada says, 'Each living thing has a different way of surviving!'

image.alt: Diversity in the Living World — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Life in the Village and Forest
slides.storyContext: Ravi finds an ant carrying a grain of rice. Maya sees a butterfly on a flower. They spot a fish in the pond, a frog jumping, a bird building a nest, and a tree growing taller every year. 'How are they all so different?' Ravi asks. 'Because each one is perfectly designed for where it lives,' Dada replies.
slides.inSimpleWords: Living things are different because they live in different places and have different ways of surviving.

image.alt: Life in the Village and Forest — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: What is Biodiversity?

points.text: Biodiversity means the variety of all living things on Earth—animals, plants, insects, fish, fungi, and microorganisms.
No two living things are exactly the same. Each has special features that help it survive.
India is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world—we have jungles, grasslands, deserts, mountains, and coasts.

example.problem: Why does a fish have fins but a bird has wings?
example.solution: Both fish and birds move through their environments, but fish move through water and birds move through air. Fins help fish swim, and wings help birds fly. Each body part is designed for that animal's lifestyle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Biodiversity is all the different living things in the world, and each one is special in its own way.

slides.title: Classification of Living Things

points.label: Animals
points.text: They eat food (cannot make their own). Insects, fish, frogs, birds, snakes, cows, tigers.

points.label: Plants
points.text: They make food using sunlight. Trees, grass, flowers, vegetables.

points.label: Microorganisms
points.text: Tiny living things we cannot see without a microscope: bacteria, fungi, amoeba.

slides.inSimpleWords: Living things are sorted into groups: animals that eat, plants that make their own food, and tiny creatures we cannot see.

slides.title: Adaptation: Living in Your Environment

points.label: Desert animals
points.text: Camel stores water in its hump; snake hides underground; lizard is fast and has light color.

points.label: Forest animals
points.text: Monkey swings on trees; snake blends with leaves; tiger is strong.

points.label: Water animals
points.text: Fish has gills to breathe water; frog has webbed feet; duck has waterproof feathers.

example.problem: Why does a snake have no legs but can move very fast on the ground?
example.solution: A snake's long, flexible body and strong muscles allow it to move by sliding and coiling. Its scales reduce friction with the ground. This adaptation is perfect for hunting in grass and hiding in small spaces.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every animal has special features that help it survive where it lives.

image.alt: Adaptation: Living in Your Environment — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Human Diversity

points.text: Humans come in different heights, skin colors, hair colors, and builds.
These differences are due to genes passed down from parents and adaptation to different climates.
Despite differences, all humans are one species and deserve equal respect.

slides.inSimpleWords: People look different, but we are all human and special in our own way.

image.alt: Human Diversity — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: A Day in Ravi's Forest Adventure
slides.storyContext: Ravi spends a morning in the forest near the village. He counts different animals he sees.

example.problem: Ravi spots: 3 ants, 5 butterflies, 2 birds, 1 snake, 4 grasshoppers, 1 tree with holes from woodpeckers, and 2 different kinds of flowers. How many living things did he observe? Name the groups they belong to.
example.solution: Total living things: 3+5+2+1+4+1+2 = 18. Groups: Insects (ants, butterflies, grasshoppers, woodpeckers = 3 types), other animals (bird, snake = 2 types), and plants (tree, flowers = 2 types). This shows biodiversity!

slides.inSimpleWords: Every time you look carefully at nature, you see the amazing variety of life.

image.alt: A Day in Ravi's Forest Adventure — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Biodiversity is the variety of all living things on Earth.
Living things are grouped into animals, plants, and microorganisms.
Each animal has special adaptations to survive in its environment.
Humans also have diversity, and all humans deserve respect.

slides.inSimpleWords: The world is full of different living things, and each one is specially designed for where it lives.

image.alt: What We Learned — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Your Turn: Observe Biodiversity Around You
slides.storyContext: Go to a park, garden, or forest near you. Spend 15 minutes observing. Count how many different animals and plants you can find. List them by group (insects, birds, reptiles, plants, etc.).

example.problem: You find a mosquito, a butterfly, a dog, and a mango tree. Sort them into groups.
example.solution: Insects: mosquito, butterfly. Animals (mammals): dog. Plants: mango tree. This shows biodiversity in even a small area!

slides.inSimpleWords: Take time to look at nature carefully. You will be amazed at the variety of life around you.

image.alt: Your Turn: Observe Biodiversity Around You — Diversity in the Living World

subject: Science
chapter: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
title: Priya's Kitchen Quest: The Secret of Good Food
hook: A girl learns that eating the right food keeps her body strong, active, and healthy—and that different foods do different jobs.

characters.name: Mother
characters.role: caring parent who cooks nutritious meals

characters.name: School Nurse Aunty
characters.role: health educator who teaches about nutrition

slides.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
slides.storyContext: Priya feels tired during sports class. Her mother says, 'You need to eat balanced food to stay strong.' Priya learns that food is fuel and medicine for the body.

image.alt: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body — Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

slides.title: Food Powers the Body
slides.storyContext: Priya's school nurse explains: when you eat, your body breaks food down into tiny pieces. These pieces become energy for running, thinking, and growing. Some foods build muscles, some give energy, and some keep your body working smoothly. Priya realizes: 'I am what I eat!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Food gives your body energy, helps it grow, and keeps it healthy.

slides.title: Nutrients: What Your Body Needs

points.label: Carbohydrates
points.text: Rice, wheat, potatoes, sugar. They give energy for running, playing, and thinking.

points.label: Proteins
points.text: Milk, eggs, dal, meat, fish, nuts. They build muscles and repair the body.

points.label: Fats
points.text: Oil, butter, nuts, seeds. They store energy and protect organs.

points.label: Vitamins & Minerals
points.text: Fruits, vegetables, milk. They keep bones strong and fight disease.

points.label: Water
points.text: Most important! It dissolves nutrients and keeps every cell alive.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body needs five types of food: carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth), fats (storage), vitamins (health), and water (life).

slides.title: Balanced Diet: The Magic Mix

points.text: A balanced diet has the right amount of each nutrient.
Half your plate should be vegetables and fruits; one quarter grain/carbs; one quarter protein.
Eating different colored foods ensures you get different vitamins: orange (vitamin A), red (lycopene), green (minerals).

example.problem: Priya's lunch is only rice and salt. Is it balanced?
example.solution: No. It has carbs but no protein, fat, vitamins, or minerals. A balanced lunch would be: rice (carbs) + dal (protein) + ghee (fat) + vegetables (vitamins/minerals) + water. This gives her body everything it needs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eat different kinds of food to give your body everything it needs.

slides.title: Common Foods in India and Their Nutrients

points.label: Rice & Wheat
points.text: Carbohydrates = energy

points.label: Dal (Lentils)
points.text: Proteins = muscle building

points.label: Milk & Yogurt
points.text: Calcium = strong bones and teeth

points.label: Vegetables (leafy greens, carrots, tomatoes)
points.text: Vitamins & minerals = healthy body

points.label: Ghee & Oil
points.text: Fats = energy storage

points.label: Fruits (mango, banana, orange, guava)
points.text: Vitamins & fiber = digestion and immunity

slides.inSimpleWords: Indian foods like rice, dal, milk, vegetables, and fruits have all the nutrients your body needs.

slides.title: Digestion: How Your Body Uses Food

points.text: Mouth: teeth chew food into small pieces; saliva starts breaking it down.
Stomach: strong acids and muscles turn food into a paste.
Small intestine: absorbs nutrients into the blood.
Large intestine: takes back water; leftover waste becomes stool.
This whole journey takes 24-30 hours!

example.problem: You eat a banana. Trace its path through your body.
example.solution: Mouth: teeth break it; saliva mixes in. Stomach: acid and muscles turn it into paste. Small intestine: sugars and minerals enter blood. Large intestine: water is absorbed. Leftover fiber becomes waste. Energy from the banana reaches your cells in 1-2 hours!

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body is smart! It breaks down food and takes out what it needs.

slides.title: Priya Plans Her Day of Eating
slides.storyContext: Priya writes down what she ate in a day and checks if it is balanced.

example.problem: Breakfast: 2 rotis with ghee, milk, banana. Lunch: rice, dal, vegetables, yogurt. Snack: apple, nuts. Dinner: wheat bread, egg curry, spinach, water. Is this balanced?
example.solution: Yes! Breakfast: carbs (rotis) + fat (ghee) + protein & calcium (milk) + vitamins (banana). Lunch: carbs (rice) + protein (dal) + vitamins (vegetables) + calcium (yogurt). This covers all nutrients!

slides.inSimpleWords: Plan your meals to include different food groups each day.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Food gives energy, helps growth, and keeps the body healthy.
Five nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins/minerals, and water.
A balanced diet has all nutrients in the right amounts.
Digestion turns food into energy and waste.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eat a variety of healthy foods to keep your body strong and your mind sharp.

image.alt: What We Learned — Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

slides.title: Your Turn: Plan a Balanced Meal
slides.storyContext: Design a lunch that has carbs, protein, fat, vitamins, and minerals. Use foods from your kitchen.

example.problem: Create a lunch using only dal, rice, oil, and water. How do you make it balanced?
example.solution: Rice (carbs) + dal (protein) + oil/ghee (fat) + water (hydration). Add vegetables or leaves if available for vitamins. This is a simple but complete meal!

slides.inSimpleWords: Think before you eat: Does my meal have energy, growth, and health?

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Magnet Mystery: The Invisible Force
hook: A curious boy discovers that magnets have an invisible power that can pick up metal from far away—and the Earth itself is a giant magnet!

characters.name: Sister Divya
characters.role: helps with experiments and takes notes

slides.title: Exploring Magnets
slides.storyContext: Arjun's toy train has a magnet underneath. When he holds it near metal scraps, they jump up! 'How does it pull from distance?' he asks. His teacher smiles: 'That is magnetism!'

slides.title: The Magnet's Invisible Pull
slides.storyContext: Arjun collects iron nails, paper clips, and coins. He brings a magnet near them one by one. The nails and clips jump to the magnet, but the coin doesn't move. 'Some things are magnetic, some are not!' he realizes. He learns that magnets create an invisible force field around them.
slides.inSimpleWords: A magnet has an invisible power that pulls certain metals toward it.

slides.title: What is a Magnet?

points.text: A magnet is an object that produces a force field, invisible to the eye.
This force field attracts (pulls) metals that contain iron.
The force works through air, water, and paper—it does not need to touch!
Every magnet has two poles: North and South.

example.problem: Arjun holds a magnet above a glass of water with paper clips inside. Do the paper clips move to the magnet?
example.solution: Yes! The magnetic force passes through the glass and water. The paper clips are pulled up. This shows that magnetic force does not need physical contact.

slides.inSimpleWords: A magnet is a thing that pulls metals from a distance using an invisible force.

slides.title: Magnetic Poles and Forces

points.label: North Pole
points.text: The end of a magnet that points north when it hangs freely.

points.label: South Pole
points.text: The end of a magnet that points south when it hangs freely.

points.label: Like poles repel
points.text: North to North or South to South push away from each other.

points.label: Opposite poles attract
points.text: North to South pull toward each other.

example.problem: Arjun has two bar magnets. When he brings them close, they spin to face each other. Why?
example.solution: If North poles face each other, they repel (push away). If North faces South, they attract (pull together). The magnets are naturally finding the position of strongest pull or push.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets can push each other away (repel) or pull each other (attract) depending on which poles face each other.

slides.title: Types of Magnets

points.label: Bar magnet
points.text: A rectangular or cylindrical magnet, strongest at the poles.

points.label: Electromagnet
points.text: A magnet made by wrapping wire around iron and running electric current through it. Stronger than bar magnets!

points.label: Temporary magnet
points.text: A piece of iron that becomes magnetic when touched by a real magnet, but loses power when removed.

points.label: Permanent magnet
points.text: Always magnetic (like bar magnets); never loses its power.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some magnets are natural and always work. Others are made by electricity and can be turned on or off.

slides.title: Earth is a Magnet!

points.text: The Earth has a magnetic field caused by molten iron in its core.
This is why a compass needle always points North—it aligns with Earth's field.
The North Pole of a compass points toward geographic North.
Migrating birds and whales use Earth's magnetic field to navigate.

example.problem: A compass is placed on a table in different positions. Why does the needle always point the same direction?
example.solution: The compass needle is a tiny magnet. Earth's magnetic field pulls its North pole toward geographic North. No matter how you rotate the compass, the needle realigns itself.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is like a giant magnet. That's why compasses point north!

image.alt: Earth is a Magnet! — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Arjun's Magnet Experiments
slides.storyContext: Arjun conducts three simple experiments in his room.

example.problem: Experiment 1: A magnet is held above paper clips on a table. How many can it pick up? Experiment 2: A magnet is wrapped in plastic and held above coins. What happens? Experiment 3: A magnet is placed inside a closed jar with paper clips in water. Can it still attract them?
example.solution: 1. It picks up 20-30 clips (depends on magnet strength). 2. Coins are not magnetic, so nothing happens. 3. Yes, the magnetic force passes through plastic, glass, and water. Magnetic force is invisible and very powerful!

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets work through materials; their invisible force is everywhere around them.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A magnet is an object with an invisible force field that attracts iron.
Every magnet has a North pole and a South pole.
Like poles repel; opposite poles attract.
Earth itself is a giant magnet, which is why compasses work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are amazing! They pull metals without touching and even guide our navigation.

slides.title: Your Turn: Explore Magnetism
slides.storyContext: Take a magnet and a collection of items (nails, coins, paper, plastic, aluminum foil, rubber, wood). Test each item. Which are magnetic? Can you find anything not magnetic?

example.problem: You test 10 items with a magnet. Nails, paper clips, bolts, and screws stick. Coins, rubber, plastic, wood, and paper do not. What can you conclude?
example.solution: Magnetic items contain iron. Non-magnetic items do not. Only iron-based metals are attracted to magnets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Not everything is magnetic! Only iron and some other metals stick to magnets.
